nameStory: The 'hooded' arrowhead gets its name from the distinctive hood-like sepals (the green leaf-like parts beneath the petals) that curve over and partially conceal the white flower petals. Like other arrowheads, it's named for its characteristic arrow-shaped leaves that look like they could have been fletched onto a hunter's shaft.
description: Hooded arrowhead is an aquatic plant that grows in shallow water or muddy shores, reaching 1-3 feet tall. It produces the classic arrow-shaped leaves that give all arrowheads their name, along with distinctive white three-petaled flowers held above the water on tall stalks. This uncommon species is part of the water-plantain family and spends its life with its roots underwater or in saturated soil.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Three white petals with curved green sepals that form a distinctive hood over each flower, giving blooms a partially enclosed appearance unlike other arrowheads

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Classic arrowhead shape with pointed tip and two backward-pointing basal lobes, feeling smooth and somewhat waxy to the touch when fresh

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Emerges from shallow water or wet mud with leaves and flower stalks rising 1-3 feet above the surface, often in small colonies

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Small, flattened fruits arranged in a spherical cluster, each with a tiny beak and feeling papery when dry

habitat: Found along the edges of ponds, slow streams, marshes, and wetlands where water is shallow or seasonally fluctuating. Prefers muddy or silty substrates in full to partial sun. Extremely rare in New England with only one recorded observation in the region.

seasonality.spring: New leaves emerge from underwater rhizomes as water warms, initially appearing as simple oval shapes before developing their characteristic arrow form.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming period with white hooded flowers appearing on tall stalks above the foliage, followed by the development of clustered seed heads.
seasonality.fall: Leaves begin to yellow and die back as seeds mature and disperse, with the plant preparing to overwinter as underground rhizomes.
seasonality.winter: Dormant period with all above-ground parts dead, surviving as rhizomes buried in pond or marsh sediments until spring warming triggers new growth.

funFact: Hooded arrowhead is so rare in New England that it's been documented only once in the entire region, making any sighting a true botanical treasure hunt discovery that would excite plant enthusiasts across six states!
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with the much more common broadleaf arrowhead, but the hooded arrowhead's distinctive curved sepals that partially cover the white petals are the giveaway - broadleaf arrowhead has simple, open flowers with sepals that don't curve over the petals.
contextualKnowledge: This species is sometimes classified under the scientific name Sagittaria montevidensis in older field guides, which can cause confusion when cross-referencing botanical resources. The extreme rarity in New England means most encounters with arrow-shaped aquatic plants will be other Sagittaria species.
compareHints: Among New England arrowheads, hooded arrowhead is unique for its curved sepals that hood over the flower petals, while broadleaf arrowhead has flat, open flowers and grass-leaved arrowhead has narrow, grass-like leaves rather than the broad arrow shape. The hooded flower structure is the most reliable distinguishing feature from all other regional Sagittaria species.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Broadleaf arrowhead stands out from its relatives by having the widest, most pronounced arrow-shaped leaves in the genus - while grass-leaved arrowhead has narrow, strap-like leaves and slender arrowhead has thin, linear foliage.
Among New England's arrowheads, grass-leaved arrowhead is instantly recognizable by its narrow, grass-like leaves – all other species have distinctly arrow-shaped or oval leaves.
While broadleaf arrowhead has classic arrow-shaped leaves and grass-leaved arrowhead has broader, ribbon-like foliage, slender arrowhead's leaves are so narrow they look like green needles.
Compared to the common broadleaf arrowhead, Midwestern arrowhead has more narrow, elongated leaf lobes and distinctly shorter beaks on its fruits.
Unlike broadleaf arrowhead with its iconic three-pointed arrow leaves, sessile-fruited arrowhead has narrow ovals.
Among New England's arrowheads, arumleaf arrowhead is distinguished by its relatively broad, triangular leaves that are wider than they are long.
Among the arrowhead family, Engelmann's stands out for its extremely narrow leaf lobes and strict preference for acidic water.
Among New England's arrowheads, Spongy Arrowhead is distinguished by its uniquely soft, air-filled leaf stalks - a feature no other local Sagittaria species shares.
Among New England arrowheads, delta arrowhead has broader, more triangular leaves than the common broadleaf arrowhead, and much wider leaves than the grass-like narrow-leaved arrowhead.
Among New England's arrowheads, this species stands out for having the thinnest, most grass-like leaves - much narrower even than grass-leaved arrowhead.
